steps.say: A jaundiced baby with pale stools and dark urine from the first days is not simply breast-milk jaundice. The bile ducts are being sealed shut by an immune attack, sometimes after a viral trigger, and associated spleen, vein and gut rotation defects hint at an early developmental insult. One baby in five to twelve thousand is affected.
steps.tx: **Biliary atresia** means **bile duct obliteration** (sealed bile ducts) that obliterates intra and extrahepatic ducts in **1** (one) in **5000** (five thousand) to **12000** (twelve thousand) infants by immune injury, viral trigger or **HLA** (tissue-type) and **CFC1** (laterality-gene) predisposition, with splenic, venous and intestinal **malrotation** (rotation-defect) associations.

steps.say: The commonest pattern seals the ducts right at the liver's front door, while rarer patterns leave the lower ducts open and directly joinable. Knowing which pattern applies decides whether the surgeon can connect bowel to open duct or must carve a drainage plate at the liver surface.
steps.tx: Type **III** (porta-hepatis seal) in the **Kasai classification** (pattern system) at the **porta hepatis** (liver doorway) exceeds **90** (ninety) percent while types I and II keep patent common or hepatic ducts and may allow direct **biliary intestinal anastomosis** (duct-to-bowel join) as **correctable atresia** (joinable pattern). Intraoperative **cholangiography** (duct dye study) assigns the type on the table.

steps.say: Still yellow after two weeks of life with a direct bilirubin above two is liver disease until proved otherwise. The workup hunts infections, metabolic mimics and thyroid failure, while the scan looks for a missing or shrunken gallbladder and a tracer study watches whether dye reaches the bowel.
steps.tx: **Prolonged jaundice** (lasting yellow) with **acholic stools** (pale stools) and dark urine from birth progressing to failure to thrive and **ascites** (belly fluid) demands liver workup through a **differential diagnosis** (cause list) if still jaundiced after **14** (fourteen) days at term, with **direct bilirubin** (liver-processed pigment) above **2.0** (two point zero) mg per dL marking liver disease. Workup excludes **TORCH** (womb infections), hepatitis B and C, **alpha 1 antitrypsin** (protein defect), **cystic fibrosis** (thick-secretion disease), galactosemia, tyrosinemia and endocrine causes.

steps.say: The illustration panels the whole disease arc: a scarred cholestatic liver, the sealed cord at the liver doorway, the loop of bowel sewn to drain it, and the giant liver cells under the microscope. Kasai's operation converts an obstructed liver into a draining one through that bowel loop.
steps.tx: **Cholestatic liver** (bile-stained organ), **atretic bile duct** (sealed cord), **Kasai jejunal Roux loop** (drainage limb) and multinucleated **giant hepatocytes** (fused liver cells) panel the disease. **Hepatoportoenterostomy** (liver-surface drainage) sews bowel to the dissected fibrous plate so bile flows directly into the gut.

vis.alt: Biliary atresia with cholestatic liver, atretic duct, Kasai Roux loop and giant hepatocytes.
vis.caption: Atretic duct, Kasai Roux loop and cholestatic liver histology. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The contrast film of the bile ducts is the surgeon's map. Normal branching trees, a clear common channel and free spill into the duodenal curve define plumbing worth joining. When dye outlines the tree on the table, the repair proceeds; when nothing fills, the Kasai plate is carved. A normal study, shown here, fills the branching tree and spills freely.
steps.tx: Intraoperative **cholangiography** (duct contrast film) with no duodenal contrast confirms disease and triggers **Kasai portoenterostomy** (plate drainage; hepatoportoenterostomy) dissecting the fibrous plate to liver capsule with **Roux en Y** (defunctioned bowel limb) drainage. For comparison, a normal T-tube study shows **intrahepatic branching** (tree filling), clear duct and free duodenal spill, the pattern absent in atresia.

vis.alt: T-tube cholangiogram showing a normal branching biliary tree with free duodenal spill, for comparison.
vis.caption: Normal biliary tree on T-tube study, for comparison with atresia. Image: Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0.

steps.say: Weeks decide the outcome more than technique does. Operating before two months saves the native liver at two years in three out of five, while waiting past three months drops that to two out of five. Every week of delay trades drainage for scarring.
steps.tx: Operation before **60** (sixty) days gives **60** (sixty) percent **two year native liver survival** (own-liver success) versus **40** (forty) percent after **90** (ninety) days, so **timing of Kasai** (operation age) decides outcome. **Age at surgery** (weeks of life) is the decisive variable, so infants must reach a liver surgeon early. Persistent jaundice past two weeks must reach a liver surgeon without delay.

steps.say: A large steroid trial answered the hormone question with a clear no. High-dose steroids after the operation did not improve drainage, brought serious side effects earlier and slowed growth. Steroid bursts are still kept for treating bile duct infection, but not for routine drainage.
steps.tx: The **START trial** (steroid Kasai study; START randomised trial) showed no drainage benefit from high dose post Kasai **steroids** (hormone drugs) with earlier serious **adverse events** (harms) and impaired growth, though pulse steroids still treat **cholangitis** (duct infection). About **45** (forty five) to **60** (sixty) percent develop ascending cholangitis on **antibiotics** (germ killers).

steps.say: The operation buys time rather than cure, bridging to transplant. More than seven in ten progress to scarring of the liver, yet four in five drained infants reach ten years before needing a new organ. Transplantation then succeeds in the large majority at ten years by both patient and graft measures.
steps.tx: Kasai never cures and over **70** (seventy) percent progress to **cirrhosis** (liver scarring), yet **80** (eighty) percent of drained infants reach **10** (ten) years before **liver transplantation** (organ replacement). Transplant gives **86** (eighty six) percent patient and **73** (seventy three) percent graft **long term survival** (10-year cure).
